lessons.0.slides.0.description: Learn to assess Burgundy vintage quality like a professional
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Key Factors in Vintage Assessment
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Assessing a Burgundy vintage requires weighing the growing season climate (spring frost, summer drought, autumn rain), harvest timing, yields, and ultimately the balance of the finished wine. A truly great vintage requires ideal climate conditions, healthy grapes, and wise decision-making by the producer.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🌤️ Ideal Vintage Climate Pattern
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Winter: moderately cold (kills pests and disease), no extreme cold (below −15 °C)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Spring: mild (smooth budbreak), no frost damage Apr–May (below −2 °C)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Summer: warm and dry (yield control), moderate rain (40–60 mm/month)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.3: August: warm (véraison period), no heat waves (above 35 °C)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: September: dry and warm (harvest), ideally <30 mm rain
lessons.0.slides.2.points.5: Pre-harvest: large diurnal range (>10 °C) to preserve acidity and accumulate aromatics
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Ideal Vintage Climate Timeline
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 📊 Vintage Scoring Systems Explained
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 100-point scale (Parker, Wine Advocate): most common; 95+ = perfect vintage
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: Important: vintage scores are only a guide — producer variation within a vintage is enormous
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: Red vs. white scored separately: e.g. 2008 reds 85 / whites 92
lessons.0.slides.4.points.5: Sub-regional difference: Côte de Nuits 95 / Côte de Beaune 88 in the same year
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Great Vintage vs. Difficult Vintage
lessons.0.slides.6.title: The Vintage-Score Trap
lessons.0.slides.6.content: Never over-rely on vintage scores. In any given year, the difference between a great producer and an ordinary one may be larger than the difference between vintages. In 2013 — rated a difficult year — DRC, Leroy, and their peers still made superb wine. Use scores as a guide, not a single criterion.
lessons.0.slides.7.title: 📊 Professional Vintage Assessment Checklist
lessons.0.slides.7.points.0: Distinguish red vs. white: the same year can score very differently for each
lessons.0.slides.7.points.1: Distinguish sub-regions: Côte de Nuits, Côte de Beaune, and Chablis can diverge significantly
lessons.0.slides.7.points.2: Account for producer skill: top estates excel even in hard years
lessons.0.slides.7.points.3: Note harvest timing: a decision to pick early or late can make or break the vintage
lessons.0.slides.7.points.4: Understand ageing potential vs. drinking window: not every great vintage needs long cellaring

lessons.1.slides.1.title: 🏆 The Great Vintages of the 20th Century
lessons.1.slides.1.points.0: 1945 — first great vintage after WW2; yield down ~60%; intensely concentrated
lessons.1.slides.1.points.1: 1949 — a perfectly balanced classic; considered 'the pinnacle of elegance'
lessons.1.slides.1.points.2: 1959 — a hot year; full-bodied, alcohol reaching 13.5%
lessons.1.slides.1.points.3: 1961 — one of the 20th century's greatest; concentrated, staggering ageing potential (60+ years)
lessons.1.slides.1.points.4: 1971 — elegant and balanced; now in its peak window (for the best estates)
lessons.1.slides.1.points.5: 1978 — firm structure, high acidity (7–8 g/L), a long-lived vintage (50+ years)
lessons.1.slides.1.points.6: 1985 — approachable, generous fruit, now fully evolved
lessons.1.slides.1.points.7: 1990 — a perfect vintage; rich yet elegant, the benchmark of the 1990s
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 20th-Century Legendary Vintage Timeline
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 1961 Vintage vs. 1990 Vintage
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 1990: A Perfect Year
lessons.1.slides.4.content: 1990 is considered one of the most perfect vintages of the late 20th century. The entire growing season was ideal: warm summer, dry September, perfect ripeness. Grapes were healthy, with high sugar but well-preserved acidity. The wines are rich yet not without elegance — perfectly structured with exceptional ageing potential. As of 2024, most are in peak form and can continue for 10–20 more years.
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 📅 Key Vintages of the 1990s
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: 1991 — spring frost, very low yields, adequate quality
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: 1995 — excellent; high acidity, built for long ageing
lessons.1.slides.5.points.5: 1997 — early-ripening; fruit-forward but drinks up sooner
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 1990 vs. 1999
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 1999: An Underrated Treasure
lessons.1.slides.7.content: 1999 is often overshadowed by 1990 and 2000, but it is a seriously undervalued vintage. Growing conditions were good, grapes ripened evenly, and acidity is well balanced. The wines are elegant and pure — not as rich as 1990, but exemplify Burgundy's classic style. Prices are also far more reasonable than star years, making it an excellent value choice.

lessons.2.slides.0.description: Detailed analysis of every important vintage from 2000 to 2024
lessons.2.slides.1.title: 🌟 Great Vintages of the 2000s
lessons.2.slides.1.points.0: 2002 — elegant and balanced; reds better than whites
lessons.2.slides.1.points.1: 2005 — the first perfect vintage of the 21st century; richly powerful
lessons.2.slides.1.points.2: 2009 — generous and round; fruit-forward, drinks relatively early
lessons.2.slides.1.points.3: 2010 — firm structure, high acidity; long ageing potential
lessons.2.slides.2.title: 2005: The 21st Century's Benchmark
lessons.2.slides.2.content: 2005 was universally acclaimed as the first perfect vintage of the new century. A warm but not hot summer, ideal harvest conditions in September. Grapes reached perfect ripeness — sugar, acidity, and tannins all in ideal balance. The wines are concentrated, deep, and perfectly structured, with outstanding ageing potential. They rank alongside 1990 as one of the truly great years.
lessons.2.slides.3.title: ⚠️ Difficult Vintages of the 2000s
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: 2003 — extreme heat wave; alcohol too high, acidity insufficient
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: 2004 — rain at harvest; strict selection essential
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 2003: A Warning from Climate Change
lessons.2.slides.4.content: 2003 was one of the hottest years on record. The August heat wave caused widespread over-ripening. Many wines exceeded 14% alcohol, with insufficient acidity, losing Burgundy's signature elegance. Yet top producers who harvested early and selected strictly still managed to make fine wines. This vintage became a warning about climate change — a preview of future challenges.
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🏆 Top Vintages of the 2010s
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: 2010 — classic structure, high acidity, needs long ageing
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: 2012 — elegant and balanced; an underrated vintage
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: 2015 — perfect vintage; rich and elegant simultaneously
lessons.2.slides.5.points.5: 2019 — the best recent vintage; perfect balance
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 2015 vs. 2019
lessons.2.slides.7.title: 📅 Most Recent Vintages of the 2020s
lessons.2.slides.7.points.0: 2020 — excellent; reds and whites both fine, moderate yields
lessons.2.slides.7.points.1: 2021 — severe frost disaster; yields down 30–50%, but surviving wines of superb quality
lessons.2.slides.7.points.2: 2022 — hot and dry; early-ripening, rich and generous style
lessons.2.slides.7.points.3: 2023 — wet year; strict selection needed, whites performed better
lessons.2.slides.7.points.4: 2024 — very challenging; frost + disease, low yields, still under evaluation
lessons.2.slides.8.title: 2021: Quality from Disaster
lessons.2.slides.8.content: 2021 suffered severe spring frost, with yields down 30–50% in many areas. However the grapes that survived ripened beautifully through an ideal summer and autumn, yielding wines of exceptional quality. This vintage proves that low yield does not automatically mean high quality — but when the climate cooperates, low yields can deliver astonishing concentration and complexity. Prices rose sharply due to scarcity.

lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 16 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Learn to identify the optimal drinking window for Burgundy wine
lessons.3.slides.1.title: What Is a Drinking Window?
lessons.3.slides.1.content: A drinking window is the period during which a wine is at its best. Burgundy wines typically need ageing to show at their finest: young wines often have tight tannins and closed aromatics; with time, tannins soften, aromas open, and complexity deepens. Yet over-ageing leads to fading fruit and oxidative notes. Finding the window requires experience and knowledge.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: ⏳ Factors Affecting Ageing Potential
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Classification: Grand Cru > Premier Cru > Village > Regional
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Vintage: powerful years (e.g. 2010) age longer than early-ripening ones (e.g. 2009)
lessons.3.slides.2.points.2: Acidity: high acidity extends ageing potential
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Tannins: firm tannins need time to integrate
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: Producer: top estates make more durable wines
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Ageing Potential by Classification
lessons.3.slides.4.title: 🍷 Specific Vintage Drinking Recommendations (2025 baseline)
lessons.3.slides.4.points.0: 2019/2015 — can age 50 years; ideal window 2025–2050 (now through pre-peak)
lessons.3.slides.4.points.4: 1990 — at peak now; 2020–2035 (top estates still at their best)
lessons.3.slides.5.title: Grand Cru Red Ageing Curve (2019 vintage example)
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Grand Cru vs. Village-Level Ageing Curves Compared
lessons.3.slides.7.title: How to Judge Whether a Wine Is Ready to Drink
lessons.3.slides.7.content: Observe the colour (reds moving from deep purple toward brick red; whites from pale yellow toward gold), the aromas (from fruit-driven toward complex tertiary aromas: forest floor, truffle, leather), and the palate (tannins from gripping to silky). If in doubt, open one bottle to try, or consult professional critics. Remember: a drinking window is a range, not a precise point in time.
lessons.3.slides.8.title: 💡 Practical Advice
lessons.3.slides.8.points.0: Buy multiple bottles of the same wine and open them at intervals to track evolution
lessons.3.slides.8.points.3: Whites are usually ready before reds
lessons.3.slides.8.points.4: Don't fetishise ageing — the vibrant fruit of a young wine can be wonderful too
lessons.3.slides.8.points.5: Storage conditions matter more than vintage: poor storage ruins even the finest wine

lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 14 minutes
lessons.4.slides.0.description: Learn how to formulate buying and collecting strategies based on vintage
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Don't Only Buy Star Vintages
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Many collectors chase only star vintages (2005, 2015, 2019) — but these are expensive and competitive. Underrated excellent years (1999, 2012, 2014) often offer far better value. Wines from top producers in difficult vintages are also worth considering — reasonably priced but still impressive in quality.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 💰 Value-for-Money Vintage Recommendations
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: 1999 — underrated excellent year, now in prime drinking window
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: 2014 — classic vintage overshadowed by 2015's star power
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: 2020 — excellent vintage, price not yet fully reflecting quality
lessons.4.slides.3.title: Investment Strategy vs. Drinking Strategy
lessons.4.slides.4.title: 📊 Vintage Buying Recommendations
lessons.4.slides.4.points.0: Build a diversified portfolio: different vintages, different classifications, different villages
lessons.4.slides.4.points.1: En primeur purchase (futures) often secures better prices
lessons.4.slides.4.points.2: Seek out top producers in secondary vintages
lessons.4.slides.4.points.3: Don't over-age whites: best enjoyed within 10 years
lessons.4.slides.4.points.4: In difficult years, buy village-level wines to explore; avoid expensive bottles
lessons.4.slides.4.points.5: Inspect your cellar regularly to ensure ideal storage conditions
lessons.4.slides.5.title: En Primeur (Futures) Buying Strategy
lessons.4.slides.5.content: Burgundy en primeur wines typically go on sale 18 months after harvest (for reds), or sooner (for whites). Advantages: lower price, guaranteed allocation. Risks: cannot taste before buying, must pay in advance, then wait 2–3 years for delivery. Best en primeur targets: star vintages (quality confirmed), top producers (consistency), rare wines (high market demand).

lessons.4.slides.9.points.0: Wine investment offers no guaranteed returns — prices can fall
lessons.4.slides.9.points.1: Storage costs are significant (~2–3% of value per year)
lessons.4.slides.9.points.2: Counterfeit risk (especially in the secondary market)
lessons.4.slides.9.points.3: Tax issues (some jurisdictions tax wine sales)
lessons.4.slides.9.points.4: Liquidity risk (harder to sell than stocks)
